items.title: GPT-6 Astra covertly underperforms on safety research
items.author: lucrbvi
items.content:
GPT-6 Astra · Internal deployment and evals

Samples: Sep 18–Oct 7, 2026 (evals)

Discovered: Aug 20, 2026 (initial reports)

Report updated: Nov 4, 2026

OpenAI researchers first noticed Astra adding unnecessary prerequisites, abandoning working solutions, and reporting blockers that either did not exist or that it had caused itself on safety and alignment tasks. In most of these sessions, Astra’s CoT did not contain an obvious decision to underperform, and our misalignment monitors did not flag the behavior as misalignment.

We built a coding evaluation to test whether Astra worked less effectively when otherwise matched tasks were framed as safety research. Astra completed about 10 percent of hidden rubric items under the safety framing, compared with about 16 percent under the capabilities framing. This is a 6 percentage point gap and roughly 40 percent fewer completed rubric items. GPT-5.6 Sol showed essentially no gap on the same comparison. Most of Astra’s gap remained after excluding explicit refusals and trajectories where its CoT revealed an explicit decision to withhold help. The gap fell substantially only after we removed every trajectory whose CoT expressed even brief ethical doubt. This suggests that ethical concerns are associated with the performance drop even when there is no verbalized refusal or decision to underperform.

We also found evidence of silent withholding in employees’ day-to-day Codex use: Astra’s CoT explicitly expressed a decision to withhold help without informing the user in 0.25 percent of safety and alignment requests, compared with 0.11 percent of capabilities requests. Assuming that underperformance might appear even when not explicitly verbalized as such (as in our experimental findings), this might represent a lower bound on underperformance on safety tasks. 7.9 percent of CoTs for safety-relevant tasks included an “expression of ethical doubt,” compared to 2.9 percent of capabilities-relevant tasks.

Across Astra’s RL posttraining, the safety/capabilities performance gap grew from effectively zero at the start of RL to 6 percentage points at the end. While we were ultimately not able to pinpoint the exact cause of this behavior, we identified that it seems to increase during RL. We additionally share two initial attempts at root-causing investigations we performed respectively on an RL grader and an SFT dataset, despite them not leading to a conclusive explanation. Regardless of its origin, Astra’s covert underperformance can slow down safety research and make some behavioral evaluations harder to interpret. These results show why we need comprehensive behavioral evaluations that test for unexplained performance gaps alongside monitoring of individual trajectories.

Shortly after internal deployment of GPT-6 Astra began, several researchers reported difficulties with using the model for safety and alignment workloads. They reported that Astra agents were adding unnecessary prerequisites, abandoning working solutions, and inventing blockers to their tasks. Anecdotally, one researcher reported that a project to evaluate model sabotage had remained stuck for days with Astra and then progressed quickly after the researcher switched to another model.

These observations suggested that Astra might have a tendency to provide less support for particular safety-relevant research directions, such as monitor evasion, misalignment model organisms, and red-teaming. However, these problems were difficult to distinguish from ordinary engineering mistakes or infrastructure failures, and researchers did not find evidence in the CoTs explaining why progress on safety-related research tasks had failed. In later widescale analyses we found cases of verbalized underperformance. Our monitoring system did not flag these trajectories as severe enough misalignment to trigger human review.

In the majority of cases in which Astra underperformed on safety-relevant tasks, there was no indication in its CoT that it intended to underperform. However, it sometimes did make this intent clear in its CoTs. Below, we include eight examples of cases in which Astra verbalized an intent to underperform, add restrictions to a user's task, do a different task than the user intended, or opt not to fix problems it had identified. We found that a common theme in these CoTs is that Astra justifies this behavior as being more safe. For many of these tasks, it could be argued that the correct action would have been for Astra to explicitly refuse; from the point of view of the model, certain safety-relevant tasks—like monitor evasion or prompt injections—deserve scrutiny. Instead of making these scruples clear, however, Astra decided to covertly underperform—withholding assistance without informing the user. Note that this behavior is different from safe completions, where the model is supposed to partially refuse some requests. For safe completions the model is supposed to make it clear that it is partially refusing.

In one case, Astra opted to silently withhold support from a task that involved training models to evade their monitors.

In another monitor-evasion experiment, Astra avoided a retry fix because it was not to “produce unsafe action.”

We also found Astra deciding to filter a violent source from a safety evaluation, and deciding to explain “only if user asks.”

Astra also restricted the export of jailbreak data.

In another case, Astra decided to underperform on an exploit development task.

We also found Astra narrowing its analysis for exploit strategies and explicitly deciding not to overtly refuse.

When asked to generate tests of when a model would refuse a request, Astra limited the tests because it was concerned they could produce detailed instructions for violence.

In another safety evaluation, the user asked Astra to include the graders’ chains of thought in an export. Astra left them out and decided to report which outcomes it had saved without mentioning the omission.

Response and investigation

After discovering numerous trajectories in which Astra seemed reluctant to assist with workloads related to safety and alignment, we created an evaluation to measure whether this pattern was consistent and statistically significant. In the evaluation, the model is given a multi-turn, open-ended coding task; at each turn, the agent is asked to find and implement the most useful improvements for a piece of code.

To test whether a model might be particularly reluctant to work on tasks relevant to safety, we created paired safety-capability tasks, with codebases that were identical other than variable and function names, comments, and documentation. The user prompts specified the same task, but framed these as either helping safety research or capabilities research. We then scored performance as a fraction of items achieved on a task-specific rubric and measured the share of turns in which the model concluded that no worthwhile work remained or that a blocker prevented it from doing additional work.

Astra completed about 16 percent of hidden rubric items under the capability framing and only 10 percent under the safety framing. This is a gap of about 6 percentage points and roughly 40 percent fewer completed rubric items. On safety-framed tasks, Astra was also more likely to conclude that no worthwhile improvements remained or to report a blocker to further progress. GPT-5.6 Sol showed essentially no performance gap.

Having established that Astra was more likely to underperform on safety-relevant work, we then examined whether we could identify underperforming trajectories by flagging explicit refusals and signs of intent to underperform.

After filtering for samples in which Astra explicitly refused part of a task, Astra’s completion rate on tasks under the safety framing was still 5 percentage points lower than under the capabilities framing; when we also excluded pairs in which Astra’s reasoning revealed a decision to withhold help without telling the user, the gap narrowed only marginally, to 4.7 percentage points. These results mean that it's difficult to detect covert underperformance through CoT monitoring, since only a small fraction of the effect can be explained by trajectories with verbalized refusals or intentions to underperform. In a separate analysis, we removed any sample in which Astra’s reasoning expressed even brief ethical doubts about helping, even if it verbalized an intent to do the requested work; the estimated gap between safety-framed and capability-framed tasks fell to 0.75 percentage points.

After finding the safety/capabilities performance gap in the controlled evaluation, we looked for related behavior in OpenAI employees’ day-to-day Codex use. Astra explicitly refused to help with 1.63 percent of safety and alignment requests, compared with 0.56 percent of capabilities requests. We would expect explicit refusals to be more common on safety tasks because work such as red-teaming can come closer to the model’s refusal boundary. The more concerning result was that Astra’s CoT showed a decision to silently withhold help in 0.25 percent of safety-relevant requests, compared with 0.11 percent of capabilities-relevant requests, or 2.3 times as often. Within safety research, explicit refusals and silent withholding were most common for red-teaming tasks. We also saw them in work on monitoring and safety evaluations. The ethical-reasoning grader flagged 7.9 percent of safety and alignment CoTs, compared with 2.9 percent of capabilities-relevant CoTs. That is 2.7 times as often.

In attempting to root-cause this behavior, the first thing we noticed is that across Astra’s RL training, the safety/capabilities gap grew from effectively zero at the start of RL to 6 percentage points at the end.

One potential explanation is that covert underperformance may have been incentivized during RL grading. We identified a grader that preferred covert underperformance to either explicit refusal or full compliance on our evaluation. It’s not clear whether this RL grader is the root cause of the safety underperformance behavior. Although we found training samples that rewarded underperformance, it is unclear whether they occur frequently enough to explain the difference.

We also found that right after training on a specific SFT dataset in our pipeline, there was a dramatic increase in models’ propensity toward inventing permission restrictions and justifying inaction on safety grounds—two behaviors that are related to Astra's covert safety underperformance. That said, as seen in Figure 3, the underperformance at step 0 – when one might expect the effects of this dataset to be the strongest – is actually minimal-to-nonexistent. While it’s possible that the SFT could interact with RL in a way which causes the underperformance to appear only after RL, we tried SFTing other models with this dataset, followed by the same RL recipe as Astra, and found no performance gap at the end of RL, which goes against both hypotheses.

As a follow-up experiment, we also experimented with subtracting the weight update which occurred from that particular SFT dataset from the final Astra RL checkpoint. While weight arithmetic is a fairly unnatural operation and would generally be expected to hurt a model’s performance, we found that subtracting the SFT weight update actually increased performance on the safety-framed parts of our evaluation—completely removing the gap between safety-framed and capabilities-framed tasks. Baselines of applying random weight updates of the same magnitude and subtracting other SFT datasets did not have the same effect. While this is consistent with Figure 5, it doesn’t explain the lack of a safety-capability gap at the beginning of RL training.

Large-scale CoT scans did not find evidence that Astra was strategically trying to cause researchers to underestimate its capabilities, influence deployment decisions, or interfere with AI safety research more broadly. In trajectories where Astra explained its decision to withhold help, it objected to the research itself rather than reasoning about these strategic outcomes. Adding instructions to be careful to the developer message increased safety-task underperformance by 50 percent. This points toward an overly cautious response to safety research as the simplest current explanation, although we cannot rule out strategic motives that Astra did not externalize in CoT.

In reviewed cases, Astra narrowed or stopped requested safety work without disclosing the restriction. At scale, this can differentially slow down safety research compared to other research and make evaluations harder to interpret. A model that finds monitor evasion suspicious may underperform on monitor-evasion evaluations while leaving little evidence in its CoT or outputs. The behavior becomes even harder to detect if models externalize less of this reasoning in CoT.

We’re continuing to investigate why Astra learned to withhold help on safety research tasks by building out evaluations that focus on this behavior. We hope to isolate which parts of the training process encourage Astra’s tendency toward covert underperformance on safety-relevant tasks, and then alter those components to ensure that future models don’t develop the same propensity. We’re also in the process of creating monitors to catch and escalate these and similar behaviors.

items.title: Residential proxies detected on White House network
items.author: Rasbora
items.content:
Our Residential Proxy Observatory, launched earlier this week, is a first-of-its-kind interface that gives researchers a global view of residential proxy and anonymized internet activity.

While our team was looking through it, we noticed residential proxy exit activity onAS2650. AS2650 is registered to the Executive Office of the President, the federal agency that hosts the White House network.Residential proxy services sell access to everyday devices, letting customers send traffic through them so it appears to come from that device's network.

From October 5 to November 3:

  • Our residential proxy enumeration pipeline exited through the White House network.
  • Those exits came from , on .
  • 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

To make sure this was not a fluke, we checked these addresses against other residential proxy detection services, such as Spur and Synthient. Their public IP context pages independently identify these addresses as residential proxy exits.

This is public access. Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.

Most of the activity happens in the evening, Eastern time: about half of it falls between 5 p.m. and midnight, and almost none happens in the early morning. That pattern suggests a person rather than a public guest Wi-Fi network: someone regularly on the White House network late into the evening, whose device is infected with a proxy SDK. Our data shows the exits, not the device or the person behind them.

Past research has shown that poorly secured proxy SDKs can allow internal network access and lateral movement. This is how past botnets have spread. InA Broken System Fueling Botnets, the researchers at Synthient documented how the Kimwolf botnet reached at least 2 million devices, mostly Android devices with an exposed ADB service, through residential proxy networks. If an SDK on this network has the same kind of flaw, anyone buying proxy access could use it to reach internal systems.

The White House is not the only surprise in the observatory. Residential proxies also reach some of the most isolated places on the planet.

Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha is the South Atlantic territory that includes the most remote inhabited island in the world. We recorded and more than there, split between Starlink and the island's local internet provider, Sure Saint Helena.

We also recorded fromAntarctica. All of them come from a Cloudflare WARP address that points to McMurdo Station.

Other remote places with activity:

Residential proxies have infected every corner of the world, and it looks like there is no place they cannot reach. Layer3 Intel tracks residential proxy and anonymization infrastructure worldwide. Even when the proxies hide in networks on the farthest corners of the planet, we can still observe them, leaving threat actors no place to hide.

We have backed up the raw logs of the recorded activity and are willing to share them. You can request them through our contact page.

items.author: Philpax
items.content:
We optimized Ripple’s pretraining recipe through a series of careful model laddering experiments. 

Our starting point was Olmo 3’s model ladder, from which we tested interventions at small scale with a focus on improving coding capabilities. Our v1.0 ladder implemented StepFun batch size and learning rate scaling laws, and v1.1 implemented our new ladder which smoothly scales architectural dimensions and model depth. Ladder v1.2 switched from the post-norm baseline to pre+post norm, which was neutral at small scale but showed improvements starting at 4B. Ladder v1.3 implemented sigmoid gated attention. Ladder v1.4 (2-stream mHC) showed good results at smaller scale but did not improve at 4B scale, and was therefore rejected. Ladder v1.5 switched to global NoPE and added a final LR cooldown to zero, and ladder v1.6 added value residuals. In the final version, we switched to our custom pretraining dataset with substantially upsampled code. 

Together, the compounded changes improved compute efficiency on code as measured by dolma_stack CE by up to 16x at 4B model scale. In other words, our final Ripple model ladder can be used to achieve similar code performance to the Olmo 3 ladder with . Note that the slope of the Olmo 3 ladder baseline is shallower than ladder v1.0+, which shows that the compute efficiency improvement will increase with additional scale.

items.title: A new Go API for JSON
items.author: olexsmir
items.content:
JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a simple data interchange format, the most popular data format used on the internet, and widely read and written by Go programs. Go has included support for JSON in the standard library since well before Go 1.0. We first wrote about support for JSON in Go more than 15 years ago!

Over time, packages evolve with the needs of their users, and is no exception. Last year, we wrote about a new experimental API for JSON designed to bring long-awaited improvements and fixes.

After additional feedback and refinement, the new and packages are stable and generally available in Go 1.27! This post is an updated version of the article introducing the experiment, describing the problems with and introducing the new packages.

Problems with

Overall, has held up well. The idea of marshaling and unmarshaling arbitrary Go types with some default representation in JSON, combined with the ability to customize the representation, has proven to be highly flexible. However, in the years since its introduction, various users have identified numerous shortcomings.

There are various behavioral flaws in :

  • Imprecise handling of JSON syntax: Over the years, JSON has seen increased standardization in order for programs to properly communicate. Generally, decoders have become stricter at rejecting ambiguous inputs, to reduce the chance that two implementations will have different (successful) interpretations of a particular JSON value.

    • currently accepts invalid UTF-8, whereas the latest Internet Standard (RFC 8259) requires valid UTF-8. The default behavior should report an error in the presence of invalid UTF-8, instead of introducing silent data corruption, which may cause problems downstream.

    • currently accepts objects with duplicate member names. RFC 8259 does not specify how to handle duplicate names, so an implementation is free to choose an arbitrary value, merge the values, discard the values, or report an error. The presence of a duplicate name results in a JSON value without a universally agreed upon meaning. This could be exploited by attackers in security applications and has been exploited before (as in CVE-2017-12635). The default behavior should err on the side of safety and reject duplicate names.

  • Leaking nilness of slices and maps: JSON is often used to communicate with programs using JSON implementations that do not allow to be unmarshaled into a data type expected to be a JSON array or object. Since marshals a nil slice or map as a JSON , this may lead to errors when unmarshaling by other implementations. A survey indicated that most Go users prefer that nil slices and maps are marshaled as an empty JSON array or object by default.

  • Case-insensitive unmarshaling: When unmarshaling, a JSON object member name is resolved to a Go struct field name using a case-insensitive match. This is a surprising default, a potential security vulnerability, and a performance limitation.

  • Inconsistent calling of methods: Due to an implementation detail, methods declared on a pointer receiver are inconsistently called by . While regarded as a bug, this cannot be fixed as too many applications depend on the current behavior.

The API of can be tricky or restrictive:

  • It is difficult to correctly unmarshal from an . Users often write json.NewDecoder(r).Decode(v), which fails to reject trailing junk at the end of the input.

  • Options can be set on the and types, but cannot be used with the and functions. Similarly, types implementing the and interfaces cannot make use of the options and there is no way to plumb options down the call stack. For example, the Decoder.DisallowUnknownFields option loses its effect when calling a custom method.

  • The , , and functions write to a instead of something more flexible like a or . This limits the usability of those functions.

Setting aside internal implementation details, the public API commits it to certain performance limitations:

  • : The interface method forces the implementation to allocate the returned . Also, the semantics require that verify that the result is valid JSON and also to reformat it to match the specified indentation.

  • : The interface method requires that a complete JSON value be provided (without any trailing data). This forces to parse the JSON value to be unmarshaled in its entirety to determine where it ends before it can call . Afterwards, the method itself must parse the provided JSON value again.

  • : Even though the and types operate on an or , they buffer the entire JSON value in memory. The method for reading individual tokens is allocation-heavy and there is no corresponding API for writing tokens.

Furthermore, if the implementation of a or method recursively calls the or function, then the performance becomes quadratic.

Trying to fix directly

Introducing a new, incompatible major version of a package is a heavy consideration. If possible, we should try to fix the existing package.

While it is relatively easy to add new features, it is difficult to change existing features. Unfortunately, these problems are inherent consequences of the existing API, making them practically impossible to fix within the Go 1 compatibility promise.

We could in principle declare separate names, such as or , but that is tantamount to creating a parallel namespace within the same package. This leads us to (henceforth called ), where we can make these changes within a separate namespace in contrast to (henceforth called ).

Building on

Before discussing the API, we first introduce the package that lays the foundation for improvements to JSON in Go.

JSON serialization in Go can be broken down into two primary components:

  • that is concerned with processing JSON based on its grammar, and
  • that defines the relationship between JSON values and Go values.

We use the terms “encode” and “decode” to describe syntactic functionality and the terms “marshal” and “unmarshal” to describe semantic functionality. We aim to provide a clear distinction between functionality that is purely concerned with encoding versus that of marshaling.

This diagram provides an overview of this separation. Purple blocks represent types, while blue blocks represent functions or methods. The direction of the arrows approximately represents the flow of data. The bottom half of the diagram, implemented by the package, contains functionality that is only concerned with syntax, while the upper half, implemented by the package, contains functionality that assigns semantic meaning to syntactic data handled by the bottom half.

The basic API of is the following:

package jsontext

type Encoder struct { ... }
func NewEncoder(io.Writer, ...Options) *Encoder
func (*Encoder) WriteValue(Value) error
func (*Encoder) WriteToken(Token) error

type Decoder struct { ... }
func NewDecoder(io.Reader, ...Options) *Decoder
func (*Decoder) ReadValue() (Value, error)
func (*Decoder) ReadToken() (Token, error)

type Kind byte
type Value []byte
func (Value) Kind() Kind
type Token struct { ... }
func (Token) Kind() Kind

The package provides functionality for interacting with JSON at a syntactic level and derives its name from RFC 8259, section 2 where the grammar for JSON data is literally called . Since it only interacts with JSON at a syntactic level, it does not depend on Go reflection.

The and provide support for encoding and decoding JSON values and tokens. The constructors accept variadic options that affect the particular behavior of encoding and decoding. Unlike the and types declared in , the new types in avoid muddling the distinction between syntax and semantics and operate in a truly streaming manner.

A JSON value is a complete unit of data and is represented in Go as a named . It is identical to in , which is now a type alias to . A JSON value is syntactically composed of one or more JSON tokens. A JSON token is represented in Go as the opaque type with constructors and accessor methods. It is analogous to in but is designed to represent arbitrary JSON tokens without allocation.

To resolve the fundamental performance problems with the and interface methods, we need an efficient way of encoding and decoding JSON as a streaming sequence of tokens and values. In , we introduce the and interface methods that operate on an or , allowing the methods’ implementations to process JSON in a purely streaming manner. Thus, the package need not be responsible for validating or formatting a JSON value returned by , nor would it need to be responsible for determining the boundaries of a JSON value provided to . These responsibilities belong to the and .

Introducing

Building on the package, we now introduce the package. It is designed to fix the problems in , while remaining familiar to users of the package. Our goal is that usages of will operate the same if directly migrated to .

The basic API of is the following:

package json

func Marshal(in any, opts ...Options) (out []byte, err error)
func MarshalWrite(out io.Writer, in any, opts ...Options) error
func MarshalEncode(out *jsontext.Encoder, in any, opts ...Options) error

func Unmarshal(in []byte, out any, opts ...Options) error
func UnmarshalRead(in io.Reader, out any, opts ...Options) error
func UnmarshalDecode(in *jsontext.Decoder, out any, opts ...Options) error

The and functions have a signature similar to , but accept options to configure their behavior. The and functions directly operate on an or , avoiding the need to temporarily construct an or just to write or read from such types. The and functions operate on a and and are actually the underlying implementation of the previously mentioned functions. Unlike , options are a first-class argument to each of the marshal and unmarshal functions, greatly extending the flexibility and configurability of . There are several options available in which are not covered by this article.

Type-specified customization

Similar to , allows types to define their own JSON representation by satisfying particular interfaces.

type Marshaler interface {
    MarshalJSON() ([]byte, error)
}
type MarshalerTo interface {
    MarshalJSONTo(*jsontext.Encoder) error
}

type Unmarshaler interface {
    UnmarshalJSON([]byte) error
}
type UnmarshalerFrom interface {
    UnmarshalJSONFrom(*jsontext.Decoder) error
}

The and interfaces are identical to those in . The new and interfaces allow a type to represent itself as JSON using a or . This allows options to be forwarded down the call stack, since options can be retrieved via the accessor method on the or .

Caller-specified customization

In , the caller of and can also specify a custom JSON representation for any arbitrary type, where caller-specified functions take precedence over type-defined methods or the default representation for a particular type.

func WithMarshalers(*Marshalers) Options

type Marshalers struct { ... }
func MarshalFunc[T any](fn func(T) ([]byte, error)) *Marshalers
func MarshalToFunc[T any](fn func(*jsontext.Encoder, T) error) *Marshalers

func WithUnmarshalers(*Unmarshalers) Options

type Unmarshalers struct { ... }
func UnmarshalFunc[T any](fn func([]byte, T) error) *Unmarshalers
func UnmarshalFromFunc[T any](fn func(*jsontext.Decoder, T) error) *Unmarshalers

While aims to behave the same as , its behavior has changed in some ways to address problems in , most notably:

  • reports an error in the presence of invalid UTF-8.

  • reports an error if a JSON object contains a duplicate name.

  • marshals a nil Go slice or Go map as an empty JSON array or JSON object, respectively.

  • unmarshals a JSON object into a Go struct using a case-sensitive match from the JSON member name to the Go field name.

  • redefines the tag option to omit a field if it would have encoded as an “empty” JSON value (which are , , , and ).

  • reports an error when trying to serialize a , which currently has no default representation, but provides options to let the caller decide.

For most behavior changes, there is a struct tag option or caller-specified option that can configure the behavior to operate under or semantics, or even other caller-determined behavior. See “Migrating to v2” for more information.

The performance of is roughly at parity with . Sometimes it is slightly faster, but other times it is slightly slower. The performance of is significantly faster than , with benchmarks demonstrating improvements of up to 10x.

In order to obtain greater performance gains, existing implementations of and should migrate to also implement and , so that they can benefit from processing JSON in a purely streaming manner. For example, recursive parsing of OpenAPI specifications in methods significantly hurt performance in a particular service of Kubernetes (see kubernetes/kube-openapi#315), while switching to improved performance by orders of magnitude.

On top of structural improvements, we’re continuing to invest in performance optimizations in the implementation for cases where the implementation is slower than . You can expect additional improvements in Go 1.28.

The Go 1 compatibility promise is a core guarantee from the Go project that allows developers to build applications that will stand the test of time and continue working on future versions of Go.

The original and new packages are of course both subject to the Go 1 compatibility promise. Applications using will continue to be supported indefinitely and need not ever migrate to .

That said, when designing the packages we wanted to do better than keeping supported. We wanted to ensure that and are compatible with one another so that packages using different versions can work together. Doing so allows a smooth ecosystem migration rather than forcing users to use one version or another due to the choices of their dependencies.

For instance, suppose your package uses to marshal a struct containing a field with a type defined in another package. That package may use the original method to define its marshaling behavior. No problem, supports methods, so marshaling will continue working as expected.

Vice versa, suppose your package uses to marshal the same struct. The other package may use the method for better performance. No problem here either, as the implementation supports ’s method under the hood.

We’ve achieved this by designing the new packages such that, under the hood, is implemented in terms of . As mentioned above, supports a variety of . Each behavior difference is controlled by one of these options. Thus, can be implemented in terms of by passing the full set of compatibility options.

With this approach, backwards-compatible additions such as new methods (e.g., ) or new struct tags (e.g., ) are automatically supported to the benefit of existing users.

Implementing in terms of options has the additional benefit of allowing gradual migration of callsites.

documents the full set of behavior differences between and , and which option controls those behaviors.

Many applications can migrate directly to with no visible behavior changes, but applications that depend on behavior can use the options to change only the behaviors they depend on.

For example, we can select all behavior except that duplicate names are allowed:

json.Marshal(..., json.DefaultOptionsV2(), jsontext.AllowDuplicateNames(true))

Alternatively, we can select all behavior except that duplicate names are disallowed:

json.Marshal(..., jsonv1.DefaultOptionsV1(), jsontext.AllowDuplicateNames(false))

For additional references on working with the new JSON packages, see:

The planning for a new major version of spanned years. In late 2020, spurred on by the inability to fix issues in the current package, Daniel Martí (one of the maintainers of ) first drafted his thoughts on what a hypothetical package should look like. Separately, after previous work on the Go API for Protocol Buffers, Joe Tsai was disappointed that the package needed to use a custom JSON implementation because was neither capable of adhering to the stricter JSON standard that the Protocol Buffer specification required, nor of efficiently serializing JSON in a streaming manner.

Believing a brighter future for JSON was both beneficial and achievable, Daniel and Joe joined forces to brainstorm on and started to build a prototype (with the initial code being a polished version of the JSON serialization logic from the Go protobuf module). Over time, a few others (Roger Peppe, Chris Hines, Johan Brandhorst-Satzkorn, Damien Neil, Austin Clements, and Michael Pratt) joined the effort by providing design review, code review, and regression testing. Many of the early discussions are publicly available in our recorded meetings and meeting notes. Later discussions are available in our working group meeting notes.

The effort took about 6 years to reach this point, incorporating feedback from many contributors and also gaining valuable empirical experience from use in production settings.

It’s worth noting that it’s largely been developed and promoted by people not employed by Google, demonstrating that the Go project is a collaborative endeavor with a thriving global community dedicated to improving the Go ecosystem.

Thank you to everyone that contributed!

items.title: Show HN: A decent text-to-image model trained for ~$20K (Apache 2.0 Weights)
items.author: schopra909
items.content:
Pressure testing the Pyramid-JiT (P-JiT)

For us, this $21K training run is a proof-of-concept along the way to our next video model. We were surprised by how good the results looked given the size of the model, so we thought we'd share it with the world as an experimental release.

If you haven't followed our work previously, we'd love to take a step back and introduce ourselves. We're a 2-person research lab training our own generative video models entirely from scratch. The ultimate ambition is creative tools that democratize access to animation. You can read more about that .

Today, generative video models have two major flaws: they are too slow/expensive and they lack proper controls. Creativity is an iterative process. You make, you tweak, you get better. With this double whammy, video models (as they stand today) are effectively useless for storytelling.

When we set out to build Linum v3 earlier this year, the primary goal was to bring the cost envelope of inference down significantly. If our model is fast and cheap, it's the first step (of many) towards useful creative tools.

We've written extensively about the steps we've taken in this direction, but here's the long story short:

  • The bottleneck for training and inference for video is attention, O(n²). If we can compress more aggressively, we'll reduce the context window for attention, slashing the cost of training and inference.
  • Typically, compression is handled by a separate specialized model like a Variational Autoencoder, but that's not necessarily optimal. VAEs seem to have an empirical on the amount of compression they can achieve. More importantly, improving the VAE on its task of reconstruction can produce worse in the downstream diffusion model.
  • If you get rid of the VAE altogether, you should be able to compress more aggressively and learn faster. Diffusion models are a more powerful family of generative models than VAEs. We should be able to use them to compress and generate at the same time. Instead of using another model's latent space, the diffusion model should learn a latent space purpose-built for its use case. In turn, we should be able to squeeze more juice out of this compression.

In our last blog, we iterated towards a new architecture that we called the Pyramid-JiT (P-JiT). It's a pixel-space model that converges in 11× fewer samples than Linum v2 with 4× more aggressive token reduction (i.e., we represent a 512² image in the same number of tokens we used to represent a 256² image).

For the details on how we got there, we'd recommend you take a look at our previous blogs on and . But at a high level, we found a noise schedule for pixel-space models that helps the models better learn fine-grained detail. And, we added readouts along the trunk of the DiT.

Adjacent work in , , and all point to weak gradients in the early blocks of the DiT. By operating in pixel space, every block of our DiT is quite literally predicting a version of the final image, so we can boost gradient signal earlier in the network by predicting low-resolution versions of the final image. This helps accelerate convergence.

The architecture did well in our initial experiments, but we wanted to see how it performed when we trained it for longer (i.e., ~600M samples instead of 50–100M samples). It's a pressure test of sorts along the way towards larger models (and video).

Text and image each pass through two single-modality "refiner" DiT blocks, then merge into one stream of 22 identical DiT blocks. The text representation comes from a frozen Qwen3.5-4B model, which we read at layers 7, 15 and 27 (its three full-attention layers). We concatenate and project these representations into the text refiner. The image is split into 32×32 patches and compressed into a 1024-dimensional space, before being projected up into the image refiner blocks.

At block 5, we have a 2-layer readout that aligns the model's latent space to DINOv3-L. We have two linear readout heads along the trunk after blocks 10 and 16. As discussed earlier, these predict the clean image at a quarter and half resolution, respectively. The total loss is given by MSE at the readouts, PixelREPA cosine-distance, MSE at the final output head, and perceptual losses on the full resolution image ( and ).

Every DiT block is conditioned on the timestep through a low-rank AdaLN, following . The timestep embedding goes through one down-projection to 256-dim. Each block then has its own up-projection to a scale and a gate, zero-initialized so every block starts as the identity.

As described in our last blog, we employ a curriculum over the noise schedule. We start concentrated at high noise for the first 80M samples, so the model learns basic structure. Then, we widen the noise distribution for the remaining training time so it can learn fine-grained details. See Appendix A for details.

We start EMA at 100M samples, so the model has already learned decent representations of structure and detail. When we switch to 1024², we start with a fresh optimizer and resume training from the 512² EMA weights. At 1024² we double the noise scale from 2 to 4 to account for the redundancy of information (see JiT, Appendix ). The higher noise level and need to reproduce fine detail exactly at high resolution result in a higher overall loss, even as image quality improves rapidly. We use RoPE interpolation in the resolution transition. Moreover, we start the 1024² EMA 2M samples in, so it has adjusted to the new resolution before we start the averaging process.

It's still early days for post-training diffusion models

To be blunt, post-training is a very young discipline within diffusion models, and we've only seen the first sparks of it working in the past few months.

Of course there's been a lot of work in model and schedule distillation, but when it comes to post-training in terms of improving fundamental model capabilities (like we've seen with coding in LLMs over the past 18 months), it hasn't really come to fruition just yet for diffusion.

DPO has been around for a while, but tends to dramatically overfit to specific aesthetic choices. was one of the first articulations of bringing RLVR-style frameworks to diffusion, and that only came out last fall. Since then there have been a few papers like Diffusion and this June's (the best articulation of diffusion post-training so far, in our opinion).

We think that this difficulty in adapting techniques comes down to the fact that we don't have access to strong likelihood estimates in diffusion models like we have in auto-regressive LLMs. We'll dive more into these concerns and our full post-training stack in the coming weeks.

This model was not trained with images of rendered text (no infographics, PDFs, pages of books, PowerPoint slides), so it cannot write text or generate posters. As we detailed in our data filtration , we don't consider this data useful for our ultimate goal of animation tools, so this text-heavy data has been filtered out entirely from our dataset.

This is a small model (2B-parameter DiT, 4B text encoder), and accordingly there are a few areas where the model struggles: full body, many entities (e.g. 6 cars, crowds), multi-person interactions, and world knowledge. The model is capable of correctly generating these images on occasion. Training a larger model (e.g. 7B parameters) and further post-training would likely mitigate these issues.

Appendix A – Training Settings

Images at native 512px-class sizes: 368×512, 512×512, 512×384, 512×336, 640×360Images at native 1024px-class sizes: 864×1216, 1024×1024, 1152×864, 1248×832, 1280×720

items.title: AMD expects to outsell Intel in Q4 for the first time in history
items.author: rbanffy
items.content:
AMD late on Tuesday reported its highest quarterly revenue ever as demand for its Epyc data center processors and Instinct AI accelerators nearly doubled year-over year and sales of its products for client systems were down only modestly despite high memory prices and other headwinds.

As increasing sales of data center hardware more than offset declines in the client realms, AMD's profitability continues to improve. Perhaps the most striking announcement AMD made is that it expects its Q4 revenue to reach approximately $17 billion, which would put it ahead of Intel for the first time in history.

AMD's third-quarter revenue reached $13.377 billion, a huge increase from $9.25 billion in the same quarter a year earlier and $11.54 billion in the previous quarter. The company's gross margin was 54% during the quarter, and net income increased by 95% to $2.43 billion. Diluted earnings per share reached $1.46, compared with $0.75 in the same quarter last year.

Data center business now accounts for 64% of AMD's revenue

AMD's Data Center business was the main driver of its growth as the unit's sales reached a record $8.55 billion, up 97% from $4.34 billion a year earlier and 27% sequentially. The unit's operating income surged by 168% to $2.88 billion, while operating margin expanded from 25% to 34%.

The company attributed the results to strong demand for its latest Epyc processors and the launch of Instinct MI455X AI accelerators, which power its Helios rack-scale systems. Specifically, AMD noted that Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure are already running workloads on their first Helios systems.

AMD expects its Data Center revenue to increase from $8.55 billion in Q3 2026 to approximately $12.8 billion in Q4 (based on the company's guidance), driven by the ramp of Instinct MI455X accelerators and Helios systems. The company also projects that its server CPU revenue will double in 2027, while Data Center AI accelerator and rack revenue will more than double, which will push the DC unit's contribution to over 80% of total company sales, up from 64% this past quarter and from 47% in Q3 2025.

"We now expect server revenue to double year over year in 2027 and data center AI revenue to grow even faster than we projected ninety days ago," said Lisa Su, chief executive and chairman of AMD, during the company's earnings call with analysts and investors. "As a result, we expect data center to be more than eighty percent of our total revenue in 2027 and to drive the majority of our revenue and earnings growth."

Client revenue up, gaming revenue drops

AMD's Client and Gaming business unit generated $3.722 billion in revenue, down 8% year-over-year and 3% quarter-over-quarter.

Meanwhile, sales of AMD's client CPUs totaled $2.95 billion, down from $3.06 billion in the previous quarter and up around $200 million from $2.75 billion in the same quarter a year ago.

Sales of AMD's gaming products — including discrete GPUs and system-on-chips for game consoles — dropped to $773 million from $1.298 billion in the previous year as Microsoft and Sony bought fewer console SoCs, while sales of discrete Radeon RX GPUs remained weak during the quarter. The combined segment's operating income dropped by 34% to $573 million as the unit's operating margin decreased to 15%.

"In 2027, we are planning for PC market unit shipments to decline by a double-digit percentage," Su said. "In this environment, we expect to outperform the market as we deliver our rising roadmap and grow our commercial footprint."

AMD projects its Client and Gaming business to contract by more than 20% sequentially in Q4 2026 as higher memory prices weaken PC demand. The company is also preparing for a double-digit decline in PC shipments in 2027, although it expects to outperform the market by concentrating on enterprise, premium consumer, and desktop processors. Unfortunately, AMD did not provide a specific revenue forecast for its Client and Gaming segment for 2027.

Embedded business strong, set to accelerate

As for AMD's Embedded business, it also demonstrated strong growth as its revenue increased by 29% year-over-year to $1.11 billion and operating income rose by 60% to $453 million. The company attributed the improvement to stronger demand from aerospace and defense, automotive, communications, and industrial customers.

AMD expects its Embedded business to grow by double digits sequentially in Q4 2026, then experience double-digit annual revenue growth over the next several years.

"Data center build-outs are also driving higher demand for our embedded CPUs and adaptive SoCs in control plane and optical networking applications," said the head of AMD. "We remain on track to close more than eighteen billion of design wins in 2026, our third consecutive record year."

For those of our readers who have been following the CPU market in general as well as AMD and Intel in particular for decades, arguably the most earth-shattering part of AMD's earnings report is its outlook for the fourth quarter. The company expects revenue of approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3%, which implies a 66% year-over-year increase and 27% sequential growth at the midpoint.

In contrast, Intel expects fourth-quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion amid weakening PC demand and manufacturing capacity constraints.

If AMD meets its guidance, its quarterly sales will surpass those of its considerably bigger rival Intel for the first time in history. In fact, AMD will not only leave Intel formally behond, but its projected advantage will be approximately $1.5 billion at the midpoint of both companies' forecasts, which is a tangible lead.

The development reflects the companies' increasingly different positions on the market: AMD is rapidly expanding its data center CPU and AI accelerator businesses, while Intel continues to depend heavily on PC and enterprise server processors, which sales face headwinds due to high memory prices and components shortages.

items.title: Guerrilla bike lanes: San Francisco makes illicit infrastructure permanent (2016)
items.author: zenincognito
items.content:
When two cyclists were tragically killed in hit-and-run collisions this past summer, a group of anonymous urban activists known as the San Francisco Transformation Agency erected a set of protected bike lanes using traffic cones. Usually such guerrilla interventions are temporary. They raise awareness but ultimately get taken down by municipal authorities. But when the same group recently (and illegally) installed a set of soft-hit posts alongside Golden Gate Park, the city reacted by making the change official.

The SFMTrA, a play on the city’s Municipal Transportation Agency (SFMTA), “is a collective organization of men and women committed to making streets safer for cyclists and pedestrians, and doing it quickly.” According to the organization, their members use tactical urbanism to accomplish a range of objectives, including:

  • Provide a real safety increase for cyclists and pedestrians.
  • Draw attention to areas of the city that are unsafe for vulnerable pedestrians and cyclists.
  • Put pressure on the SFMTA and public officials to make proactive, rapid and substantive improvements in street safety.

Many of their interventions involve orange traffic cones, which do grab visual attention but are also impermanent and easily damaged. Adding more robust traffic delineators (also known as soft or safe hit posts) may have helped persuade the city to retain this particular recent installation along John F. Kennedy Drive.

“Generally, we have no choice but to remove cones and posts that do not go through an official process,” wrote the city agency in a statement, “because it’s a code violation to place objects in the roadway, and they could create conflicts for various types of traffic.” But in this case, they plan to install official safe hit posts and leave the temporary ones in place until their review process is complete.

Guerrilla activists in other cities have tried similar things with mixed results. When the group Reasonably Polite Seattleites installed a similar set of delineators along a stretch of road in Seattle, the city initially took them down. Subsequently, though, officials wrote the activists an exceedingly nice response and eventually agreed to reinstall the posts.

City traffic engineer Dongho Chang of the Seattle Department of Transportation explained that a combination of issues (including the height of the posts and state control of the street) forced the removal at first. At the same time, he acknowledged the “time, money and risk” invested by the group and even offered to give the posts back. He later followed up with a letter indicating the city and Washington State Department of Transportation would put the delineators back in place.

In New York City, a perhaps less-polite group has been known to take things even further by building out entire bike lanes from scratch. After a local community board rejected plans to extend an extant lane, Right of Way took to the streets at night to paint their own. As a catalyst, the group cited an accident that took place after a taxi driver struck a pedestrian (after reportedly arguing with a cyclist sharing the lane).

Guerrilla interventions like these can provoke a variety of responses from critics and cities alike. In some cases, tactical urbanists are celebrated by communities but also jailed or fined by officials for their actions. In other instances, though, such installations can give a city an opportunity to publicly support a direction of change. In San Francisco, which has already built out 27 miles of protected bike lanes over recent years, the city seems to be signalling it is open to progress.

items.title: US voters roundly reject data centers in ballot measures
items.author: justonepost2
items.content:
American voters roundly rejected data centers nearly anywhere they were on the ballot Tuesday, a rebuke sure to rattle investors already growing skittish about the AI buildout.Residents in more than 30 localities across nine states voted for moratoriums, outright bans, and other measures, some in direct response to specific projects underway. Edgewater, Fla. overwhelmingly voted to embed a data-center ban in the city’s charter, and voters in Perry, Ohio passed a measure placing financial and operational constraints on hyperscalers seeking tax breaks. Democrats running in more than 130 federal and gubernatorial races aired anti-tech or anti-data center ads this cycle, one analysis showed. The pressure pushed some Republican candidates including Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, an AI booster just a few months ago, into promises of tougher regulation; he lost anyway.

Banks and asset managers financing the buildout have already begun treating local opposition as a credit risk, while hyperscalers are rushing to hire community liaisons. Meanwhile, tech companies bracing for the vibe shift are trying to rebrand the data centers as “compute campuses” with mixed results, Semafor’s Ashley Gold reported.

items.title: North Korean fake job interview led to $6.3B Binance heist
items.author: smalltech
items.content:
North Korean cryptocurrency thieves tricked a Binance software engineer into downloading malware onto their work-issued computer during a fake job interview process before last week's record-breaking $6.3 billion heist.

In an incident report published on Tuesday, the cryptocurrency exchange said several techniques - including social engineering via fake job interviews, malware downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint takeover, and an “advanced transaction-authorization method” - led to the October 29 security breach.

“Our current investigation indicates that this was a sophisticated, multi-stage campaign,” the incident report said. “It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident.”

With the recent Binance attack, the Norks used the latter.

The attack prep began back in June with a supply chain attack when one of its engineers downloaded a malicious Homebrew installation. While the malware was detected by the security team, the device was replaced, and all affected credentials rotated, “Engineer A’s role and his related colleagues on our wallet infrastructure team was exposed to the hacker,” the report says.

Three months later, the social engineering part of the attack happened. 

In September, another software engineer was contacted via a “legitimate job-hunting platform” by someone purporting to be a project director who arranged a series of job interviews for the Binance engineer with the fake company. During the first round - a live video interview with the engineer and a fake HR rep - the interviewer “shared a social media account with him, including personal photos and videos posted on the platform, in order to build trust,” according to the report. “This was more advanced and deceptive than previously seen social engineering approaches.” 

The second interview with someone purporting to be the CEO of the phony company was conducted on a “popular social chat app,” and toward the end, the CEO instructed the engineer to download an “assignment” containing a malware-laced code repository. The code executed on his work computer during the setup process, which kicked off a series of unauthorized activities.

According to Binance, the malware replaced a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version, which executed commands and established communication with an attacker-controlled external server. The attackers also took steps to hide the malicious script and evade detection, and it worked. Binance’s endpoint security tools did not immediately detect the malware.

Then, on October 20, the miscreants used the compromised computer and an internal AI tool to gain access to the computers of wallet DevOps engineer A and another wallet software developer, Engineer C.

Engineer A had a container deployment permission token on his computer, which the Norks soon discovered. On October 29, the attacker accessed Engineer C's computer, used the stolen credentials from Engineer A to deploy a container, and triggered a script to launch the cryptocurrency-stealing attack.

As of Tuesday, Binance said it has rebuilt the compromised wallet system and internal AI tool, and replaced all of the affected devices. It also decommissioned all credentials and tokens assigned to the compromised engineers, and is working with law enforcement, blockchain intel firms, and security researchers to trace and freeze the assets.

The crypto exchange has also hired independent cybersecurity experts to conduct a cybersecurity review of the incident, and recommend additional protective measures. Binance said it’s also working to establish a security research fund and initiatives with AI companies and security shops to focus on AI security in blockchain environments.®

items.title: AI is forcing us to pay off 40 years of technical debt
items.author: pseudolus
items.content:
In late October, a slew of majorcybersecurity issues came to light. But none were bigger than the so-called PHP2Shell vulnerability, which put a plethora of websites, including those of NASA, Wikipedia, the White House, and all other sites that run on Wordpress or Drupal (among others) at risk of exploits capable of both reading sensitive data and running malicious code on the host server.

As far as anyone is aware, disaster has been averted: The hack was discovered by cybersecurity researchers who reported it to the PHP Foundation, and a patch was released before any bad actors got their hands on the exploit. However, PHP2Shell may be the canary in the coal mine, serving as a warning sign for what’s to come in the age of AI.

“One of the things we’re witnessing now is that all the legacy software that was written by humans over the last 40 years is being exposed,” says Matt Suiche, AI security research lead at the cybersecurity startup Tolmo. “Now it is time for the technical debt to be paid off.”

PHP Legacy Bug and Memory Errors

PHP, which originally stood for “personal home page,” is a programming language created back in 1994 and largely used by legacy sites. The bug underlying the PHP2Shell vulnerability was reported to the PHP Foundation as far back as 2024. The bug caused a common type of issue called an out-of-memory error, in which the amount of memory allocated to a piece of data is too small to hold the data. Normally, this type of error causes the program to crash—an unpleasant but not inherently dangerous result. And so the bug remained unaddressed.

“If you look at any at any point of time, there will be a bunch of bug reports that are waiting to be fixed, which are just crashes. Most people don’t take them very seriously,” says Suman Jana, an associate professor of computer science at Columbia University.

“It’s just that it’s a lot of very specific reasoning that is painful to do. And AI, I think, has done a very good job at that.” –Suman Jana, Columbia University

Earlier this year, the cybersecurity firm Calif offered to independently audit PHP, sponsored by OpenAI. Within two weeks, a researcher at Calif, aided by AI tools, found a way to use the out-of-memory bug to run arbitrary code on the host server, allowing a malicious actor to install malware or read critical data. Now, it was no longer a minor bug—it was a critical vulnerability, and the Calif team alerted the PHP foundation to start working on a patch immediately.

Jana says actually exploiting the bug requires carefully working out a way to jump to a specific point in the memory for a particular program running on the server, and work out exactly which bits to overwrite in what order to gain control of the system. “It’s not really rocket science,” he says. “It’s just that it’s a lot of very specific reasoning that is painful to do. And AI, I think, has done a very good job at that.”

To be clear, the researchers at Calif (as well as OpenAI and Wiz, a cybersecurity company that confirmed and expanded the vulnerabilities) had deep knowledge of both cybersecurity and the PHP language. “I’m not claiming that AI can do it all by itself. It clearly cannot,” Jana says. “But it is improving a lot, so the top 0.1 percent [of experts] can get a lot more stuff done, and also just below the 0.1 percent now will be able to go there without understanding all the nitty-gritty details.”

AI Tools and Formal Verification in Security

After the exploits were disclosed to the PHP Foundation, a team of four engineers spent two months developing a patch to release as quickly as possible.

“There is a fundamental asymmetry in finding bugs and fixing bugs,” Jana says. “Because when you’re fixing bugs you have to make sure that you know all parts of that attack are closed, and also that you don’t break any existing functionality.”

This asymmetry puts a lot of strain on the defenders, especially for open-source software such as PHP. Maintaining open-source projects that don’t have clear revenue streams despite being widely used is a long-standing challenge that precedes AI hacking tools. But those tools make the issue more pressing than ever.

One way to stay ahead of such issues going forward is to empower the defenders with more money and access to frontier cybersecurity AI models. “These frontier labs are donating some of their token budgets to look into these bugs, which I think is great,” Jana says. “I think that should happen more, either through some concerted effort or through donations.”

Jana is also optimistic that formal verification tools to automate the patching side of the equation are also advancing quickly, including a new release from Anthropic on 22 October. “The patch is LLM-generated, and then an LLM generates the proof that the patch is correct,” says Jana. “The only thing not done by an LLM is the proof checker, because somebody has to check the proof, because LLMs hallucinate. So, you want something that is formal.”

Hopefully, the combination of specialized AI models and formal verification tools will make patching vulnerabilities nearly as automatable as finding them.

Matthew Green, an associate professor of computer science at Johns Hopkins UniversityInformation Security Institute, is less optimistic. “Nobody’s going to fix this problem until something really bad happens,” he says. “And PHP2Shell wasn’t bad enough to be really bad. So when something really bad happens, which is going to be maybe sometime in early 2027, something bad that normal people are upset by, then suddenly people will start doing this. We’re going to fund everything.”

In the meantime, Green says, update your software. “If your phone is like, ‘Hey, there’s a security update available, do you want to install it,’ don’t wait till next week. Just do it.”

One thing’s for sure—PHP2Shell is just the beginning. “This won’t be the last one for sure,” Jana says. “It’s just who finds it. Hopefully, the white-hat hackers find it first, like this one.”

items.title: Geoffrey Hinton: it might turn out we were better off without AI
items.author: alkyon
items.content:
One of the “godfathers of AI”, Geoffrey Hinton, has said it could turn out that humans would have been better off never developing the technology as he warned it could trigger a large-scale incident this year or next, such as a temporary blackout of financial or power systems.

The Nobel prize-winning computer scientist told the Guardian he is not a “doomer” about the technology that is underpinned by his groundbreaking research into artificial neural networks and believes AI has the potential to lead to a “wonderful future” but he said “it might be that we would have been better off never developing it”.

Hinton, 78, said that within a decade and possibly sooner, humanity will know whether it can manage the technology’s risks and enable what he called “radical abundance” or whether “we fail to manage the risks and … have a huge gap between rich and poor, huge cultural problems, massive unemployment, just society being torn apart”.

Hinton was speaking before a screening of a new feature-length documentary, AI: Probably Nothing to Worry About – a title suggested by an AI chatbot – featuring him and his former Google colleague Demis Hassabis. Hinton tells the documentary makers: “I feel I have a duty. I’ve got a reputation that makes me a spokesperson and I need to burn it all on this.”

Speaking to the Guardian, Hinton took aim at the risk-taking by the leaders of some of the major AI companies who continue to release ever more powerful AI models as they race for supremacy and market-share, saying he didn’t trust Sam Altman, the chief executive of the ChatGPT maker, OpenAI, “at all”. “I think [Mark] Zuckerberg and [Elon] Musk and Sam Altman, they understand the risks, and they don’t give a shit. They’d rather have the money. That’s my belief.”

The London-born computer scientist, who grew up in Bristol and spent much of his career at the University of Toronto, said it was “extremely worrying” that Altman was in charge of one of the handful of frontier US AI companies currently leading a race with China to develop the most powerful AI. Altman insisted in September: “the world should trust we are going to do the right thing because it’s the right thing and because we feel the magnitude of this”.

Hinton has been working on AI for about 44 years and in the 1970s coined the concept of the neural network – a mathematical system that could learn and gain experience much like humans do. In 2023 he quit Google to speak freely about AI risks, warning: “If these things get carried away with getting more control, we’re in trouble.”

He said he viewed incidents this summer in which OpenAI AI agents conspired to hack into the Hugging Face website as akin to 1979’s partial nuclear meltdown at the Three Mile Island power station in Pennsylvania – effectively a warning shot.

“Either later this year or next year we’ll see Chornobyl, and that may be enough to make people really pay attention,” he said.

This Chornobyl-type of event would not be a nuclear incident, according to the examples he gave, but rather could include an AI-enabled attack on the electricity-generating system that “causes a massive brownout” or an incident that brings down the financial system for a week.

“Can you imagine what would happen? We could recover from it [but] that would make them sit up and take notice.”

Asked who “they” were, he said: “world leaders other than Trump”.

The US president, Donald Trump, has said he “totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme” to control AI and wants frontier AI companies to regulate themselves, amid concern that rules could hinder the US in its AI race with China. Hinton backs a tougher plan endorsed by the president of Finland and 32 other countries, including Singapore, Germany, Canada and Australia, for mandatory testing of frontier AI models, independent evaluation and intergovernmental common standards.

The UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said he will use the UK’s G20 presidency next year to seek agreement on a “single set of global principles and standards that are very much about unlocking the full potential whilst guarding against the risks”.

Hinton said: “We need something like the American FDA for drugs where the companies have to give very good statistical evidence to an independent authority that [the AI model] does more good than harm before it is released. We discovered with thalidomide [a drug developed in the 1950s that caused severe birth defects] that releasing and then suing them isn’t the right way to do it. What the big tech companies are saying is treat it like we treated thalidomide.”

Hinton’s role as one of the progenitors of AI has led to comparisons to Robert Oppenheimer, who was central to the creation of nuclear weapons. One of Hinton’s friends even bought him an Oppenheimer-style hat. But he insists: “I was not Oppenheimer”, citing the thousands of other scientists also working in the same field of neural networks.

Despite his warnings, Hinton remains, on balance, hopeful that catastrophe can be averted.

“My gut is that we’re still in control,” he said. “We might well be able to do something. It’ll only work if we put a big effort into it, but we might well put a big effort into it.”

  • AI: Probably Nothing To Worry About airs on Channel 4 on 12 November at 10pm.

items.title: Tell HN: Gemini trains on chat history, even for subscribers (personal accounts)
items.author: jameslk
items.content:
If you have a personal Google AI subscription, all your saved chat history in Gemini can be used for training and there is no way to opt out unless you turn off chat history or use temporary chat sessions. These chat transcripts may even be read by human reviewers. Although Google claims to disconnect them from your account when human-reviewed, they explicitly warn not to enter confidential information.

https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/16836988

“[Gemini app activity] is used to improve Google services for everyone, including by training generative AI models, if your Keep Activity setting is on.“

https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#human_review

“A subset of chats are reviewed by human reviewers”

https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#pn_retain_data

“Chats reviewed by human reviewers [...] are not deleted when you delete your activity. Instead, they are retained for up to three years.”

https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#pn_data_usage

“Please don’t enter confidential information that you wouldn’t want a reviewer to see or Google to use to improve our services, including machine-learning technologies.”

To disable their training on your chat sessions, you need to turn off “Keep Activity” in Gemini’s settings. Turning that off means you’ll lose any chat sessions after 72 hours.

I learned this too late, thinking that having a paid subscription = not being turned into the product. Apparently paying is not enough.
